blocks.text: It is easily understood that the melolontha is that green beetle, shining with a golden colour, which we call Goldkaefer, in LINNAEUS (Syst. Nat. T. I. vol. IV. p. 1580.) Scarabaeus scutellatus auratus.
Oedmann raised still more and weightier objections to the melolontha, Vermischte Sammlungen, Fasc. 2, p. 130 ff.

EICHHORN, in his Commentar. in Apocalyps. T. II. p. 26, holds that the hair attributed to the locusts comes from the poet's own invention, because soldiers, to whom that whole comparison in John refers, were once adorned with long flowing hair, as Jerome attests on Ezechiel. XLIV, 20: to let the hair hang down — is properly the mark of the luxurious, of barbarians and of soldiers. But since not only Jeremiah (Chapter LI, vs. 27.) calls the locusts סמר, bristling, but Arab writers too attribute hairs to locusts, I think John alluded either to the antennae of real locusts, which, as we have just seen, the Arabs call two hairs, شعران [shaʿrān], or to the hairy head of certain species. Oedmann's conjecture, Fasc. 2, Chapter 6, pp. 147–149, that the Gryllus thorace spinis erectis coronatus of Linn. (Syst. Nat. T. I. vol. [III, 274] IV. p. 2066. ed. 13), whose antennae are three times longer than the body, was before the prophet's mind in this whole comparison, is very uncertain.

"I would not wish this to have been written by a great man, for the comparison would thus be too feeble; it will not be vigorous enough even if, with others, you render horrible locust, toward which Bochart too finally inclines. For what Calvin notes, that the horses are here compared with locusts on account of their multitude, not their warlike strength, will, I believe, convince few. סוס, horse, must certainly be taken for cavalry. This is compared with ילק סמר, bristling locusts, stretching out their erect hairs, both for its multitude and dense columns, and for its warlike strength, laying waste everything, and for the darts and spears with which those forces bristled, according to that line of Virgil, Aeneid 10, 178: He leads a thousand in close array, with bristling spears. Here could also belong the gloss in the Qamus under the root سمر [smr], whose second conjugation is explained by Golius, among other things, as he swiftly brandished an arrow. The more usual notion is he fastened or fixed with nails. That nail, specifically an iron one, is called مسمار [mismār], a meaning known also to the Hebrews, in the double form מסמר and מסמר 1 Chron. XXII, 3. Ierem. X, 4. Eccles. XII, 11. The participle is ܡܣܡܪܐ מסמור, fixed with nails and, as it were, bristling. — — It is therefore quite probable that the verb סמר took on the sense of bristling from a nail sticking up, erect, projecting, so that it came to be said proverbially, סמר שערו, his hair resembled a fixed nail, was nailed. This becomes more probable from the use of שער זר for bristling hair. Cf. Genes. XXV, 28." Thus Schultens in his Commentar. [III, 275] ad Iob. 4, 15, p. 105. Jeremiah seems in this comparison to have had in view both the long and bristly antennae, which Arab writers call locks or hairs, and the hairy legs of certain species of locusts.

But I. D. Michaelis, in his Observatt. Philologg. et Criticc. in Ierem. p. 393, rightly observes that this conjecture of Bochart's is hardly probable, since מספר signifies fewness. He himself thinks those translators understood a horrible locust, i.e. a horrible and countless swarm of them, from סמר, he bristled.

That the Vulgate translator was thinking of the locusta aculeata, which ROESEL presents under the name locusta indica in Plate 6, Figs. 2 and 3, and §§ 41 and 42 of the preface to his Collection of locusts, is a hardly probable conjecture of I. D. Michaelis in the Supplemm. vol. IV. p. 1080, and in the Observatt. in Ierem. loc. cit.
Schultens will give the whole passage of Firuzabadi in his Commentar. in Iob. p. 1130.
